scenario: Community search over short user-generated posts, answers and comments. Primary metrics are search relevance (nDCG) and CTR.

papers.title: TransX Technical Report: Scaling Sequence Transduction for Recommendation
papers.authors: Xu, Da, Fang, Liyan, Venugopalan, Divya, Hsu, Sunny, Wang, Xukai, Chowdhury, Rishav Roy, Liang, Cindy, Lakshmikanth, Nishant Satya
papers.abstract: We present TransX, a sequence-transduction framework and co-designed infrastructure for scaling industrial recommendation with explicit control over model-compute allocation and execution amortization. TransX separates sequence encoding, behavior memory, and candidate-conditioned fusion into independently scalable components. Training amortizes causal trajectory computation across behavioral prefixes and fans out memory states to candidates; serving disaggregates bulk prefill, nearline refresh, and online prediction through compact behavior-memory KV. We observe anisotropic scaling returns: encoder scaling may saturate beyond moderate depth at fixed memory resolution and fusion capacity; increasing supervision shifts the allocation frontier toward candidate-conditioned fusion; and the memory resolution needed to preserve quality remains roughly stable as model capacity grows. We train TransX on click and conversion, post-train its shared behavioral interface for retrieval and preference ranking, and explore generative recommendation offline. In separate production A/B experiments, the core TransX model improves CTR by 6.02% and conversion by 4.45%, while post-trained retrieval and preference-ranking variants improve CTR by 2.96% and conversion by 1.33%, respectively, over corresponding production baselines. Under matched training conditions, the training infrastructure increases supervised-target throughput by 84%. In serving, disaggregation reduces TransX's total serving cost by nearly 80% versus colocated serving at matched traffic and SLO, enabling approximately 5X the per-request model FLOPs of the HSTU-style production baseline at the same total serving cost. At matched per-request model FLOPs, TransX delivers approximately 4X higher request throughput per H200. These results show that online serving cost need not grow proportionally with recommendation model capacity.
papers.summary: TransX caches reusable behavior memory and separates sequence encoding from candidate-conditioned scoring. Offline prefill and nearline refresh keep history processing off the request path. Its base model raised CTR by 6.02% over the production baseline in an online experiment.
papers.key_insight: Compute history when behavior changes, then reuse the state across candidates. This shifts serving work toward candidate discrimination, while introducing explicit obligations around freshness, version compatibility and recovery.

deep_reading.title: TransX Technical Report: Scaling Sequence Transduction for Recommendation
deep_reading.content:
A single user request carries many candidates, and two consecutive requests share most of their behavior history. If every candidate pushes the whole history through the model again, the longer the history and the more candidates, the more repeated computation happens online. LinkedIn's TransX encodes the user history ahead of time into a compact "behavior memory", and each candidate only has to read that memory with its own query. The paper goes beyond speed: it uses scaling experiments to ask which module new compute should go into. Online, the core model improves CTR by 6.02% and conversion by 4.45% over the production HSTU (a generative sequential recommender from Meta), and disaggregated serving cuts total serving cost to 22% of colocated serving. ==One thing should be said up front: this core model spends about 5 times the per-request compute of the HSTU baseline, and at matched compute the two have almost the same offline quality==. So a large share of the online gain comes from "the money saved can pay for a bigger model".

## 1. The problem: why one history gets computed again and again

Sequential recommenders such as HSTU process the user history and the candidates in one sequence, re-encoding the history from scratch on every request. A user can have thousands of behaviors, and each request scores many candidates, so the most expensive part, history processing, sits on the online path that must return within tens of milliseconds. Making the model bigger directly makes online serving more expensive.

The other common approach is a two-tower model that compresses the user into one vector ahead of time. But one vector blends different interests and cannot answer "which past behaviors does this candidate relate to". TransX takes a middle road and keeps a set of readable memory slots rather than one vector. History processing can be shared offline, and each candidate still reads it in its own way.

The authors split this into two coupled questions. First, which computation can be reused, and over what scope. Second, whether new compute should go to history encoding, memory capacity or candidate fusion. The model's division into modules answers both at once.

## 2. Method: encode once, extract memory per cutoff, let each candidate read

![TransX's encoder–transducer architecture (paper Figure 3). A causal behavior encoder produces one shared trajectory representation reused across requests; candidate queries read only the behavior memory built from it.](figs/2610.20913/architecture.png)

The model is a chain of three parts. The first is a causal encoder that processes user behaviors in time order; each position sees only earlier behaviors, so predicting an exposure never uses clicks that happened later. The second is memory construction: at the cutoff for each request, the encodings of the most recent $W$ behaviors are kept as-is as local memory, and older history is pooled in blocks into a few global summaries; the two are concatenated and projected into keys and values for attention, which the paper calls behavior-memory KV (key–value). The number of memory slots is far smaller than the history length. The third is candidate fusion: each candidate builds a query through the same feature interface as historical behaviors, cross-attends to the memory, and feeds output heads for clicks, conversions and so on.

Training is organized along the same boundary. Logs are usually one row per candidate, so a user's many requests store and encode the overlapping history again and again. TransX packs a user's behavior trajectory and all its requests into one training unit: the trajectory is encoded once, the memory for each request cutoff is extracted and fanned out to all candidates of that request, and the gradients from all candidates flow back into the same encoding.

On that basis, the authors first train the core model on clicks and conversions, then keep the shared encoder and memory and train separate readers and output heads for retrieval and preference ranking. Generative retrieval and generative ranking were also explored offline, but their quality is more sensitive to semantic-ID design and autoregressive decoding, and the authors explicitly treat them as exploration; they were not launched.

## 3. Serving: three clocks and immutable snapshots

![Disaggregated serving (paper Figure 6). Offline and nearline workers maintain encoder continuation state and publish compact, immutable behavior-memory snapshots; online requests read only snapshots compatible with their model version.](figs/2610.20913/serving.png)

Serving is split into three paths, each scaling with its own rhythm and bottleneck. Offline bulk prefill computes state for all active users when a model rolls out, optimizing for throughput. Nearline updates advance the encoder state and publish new memory when a user acts, optimizing update throughput within a freshness budget. Online prediction only fetches the memory snapshot, then runs candidate fusion and scoring.

Two objects are easy to confuse here. The encoder continuation state lets the nearline path resume encoding where it left off, and is about 496 KiB per user at the median; the behavior memory read online is only about 8.5 KiB. The former stays nearline and never enters the online cache. Before publication the memory is also quantized: a calibrated orthogonal rotation, then bits allocated by per-coordinate energy, shrinking the median size from 28 KiB in BF16 to 8.5 KiB, with test AUC changing by no more than 2×10⁻³.

Immutable snapshots are what make this division of labor work. A request pins a version when it starts, and when an update publishes a new version, in-flight scoring never reads a half-old, half-new state. When state is missing or too stale, the request falls back to an older compatible snapshot or a non-sequential fallback model, while rebuilding happens asynchronously in the background. In production, nearline update lag is 1.2 seconds at the median and 1.8 seconds at p90, more than 92% of traffic reads the latest compatible snapshot, and about 3% goes to the fallback model, mostly cold-start users with too little history.

## 4. Scaling experiments: where should compute go

The authors split compute into three coordinates: encoder compute per trajectory $C_E$, the memory budget exposed online $B_M$, and fusion compute per candidate $C_F$. Data are split along two axes too: history richness, cut by history-length quantiles into sparse, medium and rich groups, and supervision $\eta$ at three levels, 0.20, 0.25 and 0.30. Encoder compute is shared by many candidates while fusion runs once per candidate, so the authors first convert encoder compute to a per-training-target basis by its reuse count before comparing.

![Scaling experiments (paper Figure 7). B: growing the encoder at fixed fusion and memory resolution; C: fusion width versus depth; D: the difference between fusion and encoder marginal returns as supervision changes; F: the share of compute given to fusion in the validation-selected best configuration.](figs/2610.20913/fig7_allocation.png)

The first finding is diminishing returns from the encoder. At fixed memory resolution and fusion capacity, a bigger encoder raises test AUC in all three user groups, with most of the gain in the lower and middle part of the sweep and much less beyond about four layers. Since memory resolution is unchanged, this gain does not come from "showing more state to the online path"; the encoder packs useful information better into memory of the same size.

The second finding is that the more supervision, the more compute should go to fusion. Widening fusion from 128 to 1024 raises test AUC by about 90 basis points (1 basis point is 0.0001) at $\eta=0.30$, and by less than 10 at $\eta=0.20$; adding fusion layers saturates early. Under a fixed total compute budget, the fusion share of the validation-selected best configuration also rises with supervision, from about half to about nine tenths at the largest budget, showing that with more supervision the model needs stronger candidate reading. The authors explain this with a decomposition of log loss: total loss equals irreducible uncertainty, plus "information lost by the memory", plus "readout mismatch". The memory budget limits the first, fusion capacity the second; with ample supervision, readout mismatch is more worth optimizing.

The third finding is that a bigger model does not need proportionally more memory. The authors define the "adequate" memory budget as the smallest one within 3 AUC basis points of the highest-resolution memory. As encoder and fusion compute grow, the adequate memory density stays stable or even falls, and so does the absolute KV footprint. ==This matters for the system: the model can keep growing while the state transferred and cached online does not have to grow with it==.

Two discounts apply to these experiments. Supervision only covers 0.20 to 0.30, a span of just 1.5 times, and nearly all the jump in fusion returns falls between 0.25 and 0.30, so extrapolation needs care. The authors also state that the best allocation depends on the model family, data and compute range, and these patterns are not a universal scaling law.

## 5. Online results and system efficiency

The three variants ran independent A/B tests on different product surfaces, each against its own production model, and the authors stress that the columns are not comparable with each other. All lifts have p below 10⁻⁴ except feed views.

| Metric | Core model vs HSTU | Retrieval variant vs production embedding retrieval | Ranking variant vs production learning-to-rank model |
|---|---|---|---|
| CTR | +6.02% | +2.96% | not reported |
| Conversion | +4.45% | +0.05% | +1.33% |
| DAU | +0.26% | +0.04% | +0.10% |
| Feed views | +0.08% | +0.06% | not reported |

Split by history length, the core model's CTR lift is 5.5%, 6.0% and 6.2% for sparse, medium and rich users, showing the gain is not confined to users with rich histories. The core model also ran a five-week holdout with no decay in gains; the authors credit daily retraining and redeployment, and the training and prefill optimizations are what make daily updates feasible.

On system efficiency, training is compared on 32 H200s against a straightforward FSDP (fully sharded data parallel) baseline, with model, data and batch size fixed. Because each trajectory is encoded once, supervised-target throughput rises 84%, compute utilization goes from about 11% to 18%, and time to convergence drops from about 25 hours to 13, which is also why daily updates are possible. Online, each H200 serves about 250 requests per second with p99 end-to-end scoring latency of 49 ms.

![Serving-efficiency analysis (paper Figure 11). With cached behavior memory, p99 latency barely changes as history grows from hundreds to over a thousand records; more candidates still raise latency.](figs/2610.20913/efficiency.png)

Compared with an online path that processes history synchronously, reading cached memory cuts p99 scoring latency by 71% to 91%. Latency grows mainly with candidate count and hardly with history length, matching the structure in which heavy history computation has left the online path. Scaling an HSTU-style baseline to the same per-request compute as TransX, the two differ by less than 10⁻³ in offline click AUC, while TransX's request throughput per H200 is about 4 times higher.

The cost account needs to include the new work moved offline. Online GPU use drops from 5.8 to 1.1 GPU hours per million requests, down 81.2%; but it adds 7.5 CPU hours of nearline work per million behavior updates and 3.2 GPU hours of offline prefill per deployment. After converting all resources to a common cost basis, total cost is 22% of colocated serving. Storage and network stay roughly flat, because the online path no longer moves raw behavior history and moves compact memory instead.

Freshness has a price too. The authors relaxed the allowed update lag step by step online. Moving p90 from 1.8 seconds to 1.2 minutes lowers CTR by 0.21% and in-session CTR by 0.37%; relaxing to 18 minutes costs another 0.12% and 0.18%; beyond that, losses shrink quickly. The losses concentrate in the seconds-to-minutes range, showing that nearline updates need not be synchronous with requests, but their service level directly affects short-term recommendation quality.

## 6. Limitations and practical implications

The authors list three limitations. The scaling patterns hold only within the studied data, supervision levels, model family and deployment envelope, and do not uniquely identify the mechanisms behind them. Maintaining continuation state and memory brings freshness, storage, version-compatibility and recovery costs; some absolute costs are omitted under disclosure policy, and the numbers are not a full lifecycle accounting. A shared memory and frozen backbone are not necessarily right for every task; if a task needs information the encoder did not keep, swapping the reader is not enough.

For recommender systems with long histories, the most useful lesson is to first measure how much computation is repeated: how much history is re-encoded between consecutive requests of one user, and across the candidates of one request. If the share is high, moving history encoding nearline and reading compact memory online frees compute that can pay for a bigger model. The scaling experiments can be copied the same way: sweep encoder, memory and fusion separately, record results by history richness and supervision, and do not report only a total parameter count. On the serving side, monitor memory age, fallback share and version-incompatibility rate alongside latency and CTR.

papers.title: RecSoup: Efficient Model Merging Approach for Controllable Multi-Objective Recommendation
papers.authors: Jia, Zidong, Xie, Guofu, Zhang, Xiao
papers.abstract: Recommender systems often need to balance multiple conflicting objectives. Controllable Multi-Objective Recommendation (CMOR) enables dynamic adjustment of objective trade-offs at inference time without retraining, adapting to shifting user or system requirements. Existing CMOR approaches typically rely on output-level reranking or parameter-generating modules, which either limit the scope of feasible trade-offs or incur substantial training and inference cost. Model merging provides a promising alternative by reusing multiple objective-specific models via parameter combination. However, its direct application to recommender systems is challenging due to the lack of a shared linear regime and cross-objective interference. To address these issues, we propose RecSoup, a lightweight two-stage approach for effective CMOR via specialized model merging. RecSoup first mitigates parameter interference across objectives through a pruning strategy that jointly considers objective-specific importance and cross-objective relevance. It then performs adaptive parameter merging via a learnable preference-to-coefficient mapping, allowing dynamic trade-off control at inference time without joint retraining or additional generative modules. Theoretically, we prove that RecSoup outperforms the parameter generation paradigm in effectiveness and efficiency, as it can fully navigate the Pareto front without smoothness constraints. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that RecSoup achieves improved Pareto front quality and effective controllability while delivers 165--228x faster inference-time latency than parameter generation approaches. Code is available at this https URL .
papers.summary: RecSoup makes accuracy–diversity trade-offs adjustable by reusing objective-specific checkpoints. It prunes task-vector updates and learns preference-dependent merge coefficients. Parameter construction was about 165–228 times faster than a hypernetwork across three benchmarks.
papers.key_insight: Controllability can come from combining existing specialists. Pruning and coefficient learning solve different problems: preserving useful updates and choosing their mixture. The latency claim concerns parameter construction, not the full recommendation pipeline.

deep_reading.title: RecSoup: Efficient Model Merging Approach for Controllable Multi-Objective Recommendation
deep_reading.content:
RecSoup makes recommendation trade-offs adjustable by combining models trained for different objectives. It first prunes their parameter updates, then learns how a requested preference should determine merge coefficients. The goal is to avoid retraining or generating a large parameter set whenever the desired balance changes.

## 1. Problem and motivation

Recommendation systems balance objectives such as accuracy and diversity. A fixed compromise may be unsuitable across users, product surfaces or changing operating requirements.

Reranking can adjust a list, but only within the available candidates. Hypernetworks and diffusion-based approaches can generate preference-conditioned parameters, at the cost of auxiliary models and additional construction work. RecSoup asks whether existing objective-specialized checkpoints can provide the necessary building blocks.

Naive averaging is unreliable when objectives change overlapping parameters in competing ways. In addition, objective weights need not equal useful parameter-mixing weights. RecSoup separates choosing which updates to retain from learning how strongly to combine them.

## 2. Method: prune the basis, learn the coefficients

![Pruning refines the task-vector basis; a preference-conditioned mapper chooses merge coefficients while the base and experts stay frozen.](figs/2610.21220/architecture.svg)

Each specialist starts from a common base model. Its difference from that base is a task vector: the parameter update associated with an objective. Merging adds a weighted combination of these updates back to the base, requiring aligned parameter structures and a compatible starting point.

The pruning stage combines two importance signals. Objective-specific importance measures a coordinate's squared update relative to the vector's total squared norm. Cross-objective relevance measures the magnitude of its interaction with updates at the same coordinate in other objectives.

The cross-objective term uses an absolute value deliberately. Opposite update directions can encode an important trade-off, so sign disagreement alone is not sufficient reason to discard them. The procedure seeks useful support rather than simply enforcing agreement.

Coordinates are ranked by the combined score. The method retains enough of them to preserve a chosen fraction of objective-specific update energy. Experiments use a norm-retention threshold of 0.9–0.95; this is not the fraction of parameter coordinates retained.

The second stage trains a lightweight gate from objective preferences to merge coefficients. The coefficients need not numerically match the preference vector. Only the gate is updated; the base and pruned task vectors remain frozen. A preference-weighted loss trains the mapping on a subset of data.

![This subfigure examines cross-objective overlap after pruning, one diagnostic of the parameter basis used for coefficient learning.](figs/2610.21220/pruning.svg)

Pruning and adaptive merging solve distinct problems. The former identifies parameter support, while the latter selects a combination for the requested operating point.

## 3. Contributions and the scope of the argument

The contribution is not model merging in isolation. It is a recommendation-specific way to turn existing specialists into a controllable family of models, rather than one fixed merged checkpoint.

The authors examine accuracy- and diversity-specialized task vectors using PCA and find that updates are not concentrated in a small shared subspace. This motivates tailored merging, although PCA geometry alone does not establish all claims about nonlinear model behavior.

The theoretical comparison also has explicit assumptions. It treats the convex hull of two experts as the Pareto-optimal set and considers a parameter generator with a restricted Lipschitz constant. The result establishes a coverage limitation under those conditions; it does not show that arbitrary hypernetworks are universally inferior.

The empirical contribution is more directly actionable: pruning rules, coefficient mappings and recommendation backbones are evaluated separately through ablations.

## 4. Experiments: parameter construction is one stage

Experiments use MovieLens-1M and Amazon food and toy datasets, with three sequential-recommendation backbones. Accuracy–diversity is the main setting, supplemented by fairness and three-objective experiments. Accuracy specialists use pairwise ranking loss; diversity specialists encourage category novelty and reduce redundancy.

The table reports mean inference-time parameter construction latency in milliseconds. Standard deviations are omitted here for readability.

| Dataset | Hypernetwork | RecSoup | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| MovieLens-1M | 7.5281 | 0.0454 | 165.9× |
| Amazon Food | 9.3799 | 0.0410 | 228.8× |
| Amazon Toys | 9.2741 | 0.0436 | 212.7× |

These measurements concern constructing parameters. They exclude the full feature, retrieval and ranking pipeline, and do not establish the same speedup over every generation method. Serving impact depends on how often preferences change and how long constructed parameters can be reused.

For quality, hypervolume summarizes the objective-space coverage of the trade-off frontier. Controllability checks whether changing a preference moves its corresponding metric in the intended direction. On MovieLens with SASRec, RecSoup achieves hypervolume 0.7090 versus 0.6536 for simple merging.

The table does not show universal dominance. In that same setting, an unpruned ablation has higher hypervolume, and some retrained operating points remain stronger. Pruning is an empirical trade-off whose value should be assessed across both quality and controllability.

Training and evaluation use sampled negatives. Full-catalog ranking may change the effects of popularity, candidate scale and parameter construction costs. Released code provides a basis for checking these conditions.

## 5. Limitations

The paper's complexity analysis acknowledges that full-parameter merging can be dominated by a large item-embedding table. Generating a few coefficients is cheap, but reading and combining many parameters still consumes bandwidth.

The evidence concerns offline trade-off quality and parameter construction efficiency. It does not include production CTR or revenue experiments. Specialist training is also an existing cost, even when only a small gate is trained in the final stage.

A serving system must decide whether to merge per request or cache a finite number of preference settings. Highly individualized, rapidly changing preferences have different concurrency and memory implications from shared operating points. The latency table does not settle that deployment choice.

## 6. Practical implications

Teams with aligned accuracy and diversity checkpoints can compare simple averaging, pruning plus averaging, and learned coefficients under identical backbones and candidates. This isolates whether each stage adds value.

Community recommendation can begin with a small set of interpretable exploration settings and cache their merged models. Per-request merging is a separate experiment that should include parameter bandwidth and tail latency.

Report accuracy, diversity, preference responsiveness and end-to-end cost independently. A model can improve average quality while responding inconsistently to control inputs. RecSoup's reusable parameter interface is valuable precisely because these properties can be tested separately.
deep_reading.content_html:
RecSoup makes recommendation trade-offs adjustable by combining models trained for different objectives. It first prunes their parameter updates, then learns how a requested preference should determine merge coefficients. The goal is to avoid retraining or generating a large parameter set whenever the desired balance changes.

1. Problem and motivation

Recommendation systems balance objectives such as accuracy and diversity. A fixed compromise may be unsuitable across users, product surfaces or changing operating requirements.

Reranking can adjust a list, but only within the available candidates. Hypernetworks and diffusion-based approaches can generate preference-conditioned parameters, at the cost of auxiliary models and additional construction work. RecSoup asks whether existing objective-specialized checkpoints can provide the necessary building blocks.

Naive averaging is unreliable when objectives change overlapping parameters in competing ways. In addition, objective weights need not equal useful parameter-mixing weights. RecSoup separates choosing which updates to retain from learning how strongly to combine them.

2. Method: prune the basis, learn the coefficients

Each specialist starts from a common base model. Its difference from that base is a task vector: the parameter update associated with an objective. Merging adds a weighted combination of these updates back to the base, requiring aligned parameter structures and a compatible starting point.

The pruning stage combines two importance signals. Objective-specific importance measures a coordinate's squared update relative to the vector's total squared norm. Cross-objective relevance measures the magnitude of its interaction with updates at the same coordinate in other objectives.

The cross-objective term uses an absolute value deliberately. Opposite update directions can encode an important trade-off, so sign disagreement alone is not sufficient reason to discard them. The procedure seeks useful support rather than simply enforcing agreement.

Coordinates are ranked by the combined score. The method retains enough of them to preserve a chosen fraction of objective-specific update energy. Experiments use a norm-retention threshold of 0.9–0.95; this is not the fraction of parameter coordinates retained.

The second stage trains a lightweight gate from objective preferences to merge coefficients. The coefficients need not numerically match the preference vector. Only the gate is updated; the base and pruned task vectors remain frozen. A preference-weighted loss trains the mapping on a subset of data.

Pruning and adaptive merging solve distinct problems. The former identifies parameter support, while the latter selects a combination for the requested operating point.

3. Contributions and the scope of the argument

The contribution is not model merging in isolation. It is a recommendation-specific way to turn existing specialists into a controllable family of models, rather than one fixed merged checkpoint.

The authors examine accuracy- and diversity-specialized task vectors using PCA and find that updates are not concentrated in a small shared subspace. This motivates tailored merging, although PCA geometry alone does not establish all claims about nonlinear model behavior.

The theoretical comparison also has explicit assumptions. It treats the convex hull of two experts as the Pareto-optimal set and considers a parameter generator with a restricted Lipschitz constant. The result establishes a coverage limitation under those conditions; it does not show that arbitrary hypernetworks are universally inferior.

The empirical contribution is more directly actionable: pruning rules, coefficient mappings and recommendation backbones are evaluated separately through ablations.

4. Experiments: parameter construction is one stage

Experiments use MovieLens-1M and Amazon food and toy datasets, with three sequential-recommendation backbones. Accuracy–diversity is the main setting, supplemented by fairness and three-objective experiments. Accuracy specialists use pairwise ranking loss; diversity specialists encourage category novelty and reduce redundancy.

The table reports mean inference-time parameter construction latency in milliseconds. Standard deviations are omitted here for readability.

These measurements concern constructing parameters. They exclude the full feature, retrieval and ranking pipeline, and do not establish the same speedup over every generation method. Serving impact depends on how often preferences change and how long constructed parameters can be reused.

For quality, hypervolume summarizes the objective-space coverage of the trade-off frontier. Controllability checks whether changing a preference moves its corresponding metric in the intended direction. On MovieLens with SASRec, RecSoup achieves hypervolume 0.7090 versus 0.6536 for simple merging.

The table does not show universal dominance. In that same setting, an unpruned ablation has higher hypervolume, and some retrained operating points remain stronger. Pruning is an empirical trade-off whose value should be assessed across both quality and controllability.

Training and evaluation use sampled negatives. Full-catalog ranking may change the effects of popularity, candidate scale and parameter construction costs. Released code provides a basis for checking these conditions.

5. Limitations

The paper's complexity analysis acknowledges that full-parameter merging can be dominated by a large item-embedding table. Generating a few coefficients is cheap, but reading and combining many parameters still consumes bandwidth.

The evidence concerns offline trade-off quality and parameter construction efficiency. It does not include production CTR or revenue experiments. Specialist training is also an existing cost, even when only a small gate is trained in the final stage.

A serving system must decide whether to merge per request or cache a finite number of preference settings. Highly individualized, rapidly changing preferences have different concurrency and memory implications from shared operating points. The latency table does not settle that deployment choice.

6. Practical implications

Teams with aligned accuracy and diversity checkpoints can compare simple averaging, pruning plus averaging, and learned coefficients under identical backbones and candidates. This isolates whether each stage adds value.

papers.title: Agentic-Priors: Using Large Language Models to Address the Cold Start Problem in Preference Elicitation
papers.authors: Arcanjo, Bruno, Li, Zhaoxing, Stein, Sebastian
papers.abstract: An agent that learns a user's preferences from their choices faces a cold start problem: before any choices are observed, it must rely solely on a prior. Informative priors are usually fitted to historical choice data, which new tasks and deployments lack. To address this, we present Agentic-Priors, which lets agentic systems use the implicit knowledge of large language models (LLMs) instead. Specifically, an LLM states a new user's trade-offs in interpretable terms, such as willingness to pay or value of time, which we map to a prior over multinomial logit coefficients. This prior is then refined by a Bayesian learner as choices are observed. Across seven choice datasets, Agentic-Priors improves cold start accuracy over an uninformed prior by 5-40 percentage points. It also outperforms AutoElicit, a state-of-the-art LLM prior-elicitation method, on three datasets and loses on one. It is up to 18 points more accurate than in-context learning, and never significantly worse. Against hierarchical Bayes models fitted to surveys of increasing size, our approach is worth roughly 6-40 surveyed users, in terms of log-loss, so its value is concentrated in a deployment's first users.
papers.summary: Agentic-Priors asks a language model for interpretable trade-offs, maps them to priors over choice-model coefficients and updates them with observed choices. Across seven datasets, cold-start accuracy exceeded an uninformed prior by 5–40 percentage points.
papers.key_insight: Use language-model knowledge as an uncertain starting point rather than a fixed label. Bayesian updates allow individual observations to take over. The approach is most useful before enough historical choice data exist.

papers.title: Understanding and Mitigating Training Instability in Large-Scale Recommender Systems: A Cascade Perspective
papers.authors: Li, Yuening, Wang, Zeyu, Zhang, Zhen, Liu, Jiayi, Jiang, Zhimeng, Roh, Yuji, Xu, Weikai, Gao, Mingyan, Dalal, Onkar, He, Chuan, Liu, Liang
papers.abstract: Training large-scale recommender systems on dynamic industrial platforms, such as Short-Form Video (SFV) services with billions of daily interactions, faces critical stability challenges. Rapid distribution shifts in user data and increasing model complexity frequently trigger a divergence cascade, typically initiating with gradient explosion, propagating to weight explosion, and culminating in loss explosion. This G-W-L cascade severely impedes model convergence and performance. This paper provides a systematic analysis of this G-W-L cascade within an industrial SFV recommender context. We then propose and evaluate a structured mitigation framework where interventions are explicitly mapped to counteract specific stages of the cascade: gradient (G) control, weight/activation (W) stabilization, and loss (L) shaping. Our contribution provides a structured framework for understanding and tackling training divergence, offering practical insights for deploying robust, continuously updated recommenders in large-scale, non-stationary settings. We empirically validate the effectiveness of these strategies on a major industrial SFV recommendation system.
papers.summary: Google studies training divergence as a gradient–weight–loss cascade and maps interventions to each stage. The combined treatment improved AUC by 0.38% relative to baseline on the second binary classification task.
papers.key_insight: Inspect gradients, weights or activations, and task losses on one timeline. A loss spike may be the end of a cascade. Intervention effects differ across classification and regression tasks.

papers.title: Hybrid transformer-based recommender system with LLM-assisted semantic modeling for sequential and federated learning
papers.abstract: LLMTransRec combines item identity, genre metadata and BERT-based semantic embeddings with a Transformer for next-item prediction. Evaluated on four datasets (MovieLens 1M, MovieLens 20M, Goodbooks-10k and Anime). Federated Averaging experiments are a feasibility proof of concept, not a practical federated recommender benchmark.
papers.summary: LLMTransRec combines item identity, genre metadata and BERT-derived text representations in a Transformer for next-item prediction. It reports offline tests on four benchmarks; the federated component is a feasibility study. The accessible page does not quantify the main gains.
papers.key_insight: Semantic content and interactions can share a compact sequence backbone. The appendix specifies BERT representations, rather than an online generative model. Treat the federated result as a proof of concept.

papers.title: CalendarRec: Multi-Order Temporal Context for Sequential Recommendation
papers.abstract: CalendarRec models multi-order temporal context for sequential recommendation in health functional food e-commerce, using calendar information with state-space sequence models.
papers.summary: CalendarRec adds separate month, day and weekday representations to a Mamba-based sequential recommender. On health-functional-food click logs, NDCG@10 improved by 14.2% relative to Mamba4Rec.
papers.key_insight: Calendar position captures recurring demand that interaction order alone misses. Separate temporal embeddings offer a concrete feature-design option; the headline result is from health-food e-commerce.

papers.title: Encoded but Exposed: Language Embeddings can Reveal More Than They Should in Recommender Systems
papers.abstract: Language embeddings are increasingly used in recommenders to represent item content, but their privacy risks remain poorly understood. We study whether item embeddings can reveal item identities when an adversary has access to auxiliary item text from external sources. We show that a simple cosine-similarity attack can recover item identities with high mean reciprocal rank across language models and candidate-set settings on two real-world datasets. Leakage is strongest when the adversary's partial information overlaps with the victim representation, but it also persists through semantic alignment between independently sourced descriptions. We further show that item leakage can propagate to user re-identification from sparse ratings. Finally, we evaluate obfuscated descriptions as a mitigation and find a clear leakage-utility tradeoff.
papers.summary: Language embeddings can expose item identities through similarity matching against public descriptions. Experiments on two datasets also show that item leakage can enable user re-identification from sparse ratings. Obfuscation reduces leakage but harms recommendation utility.
papers.key_insight: Unreadable vectors are not anonymous records. Public catalogs can provide the auxiliary information needed for identification. Evaluate both item recovery and user linkage when assessing embedding-sharing risks.

papers.title: Reliability-aware ensemble recommendation for open-network commerce: a dual-metric framework for jointly evaluating ranking accuracy and serving correctness
papers.abstract: An ensemble recommender for open-network commerce separately measures ranking quality and serving correctness under catalog, retrieval and identifier failures, with fallback mechanisms and graph/neural collaborative filtering.
papers.summary: This study separates ranking quality from serving correctness in open-network commerce. In controlled trace replays, routing and identifier fixes raised route resolution success from 60.0% to 99.8%. These are reproducible system experiments, not production A/B results.
papers.key_insight: Ranking metrics cannot detect broken destinations or inconsistent item identities. Track accessibility alongside relevance. The study tests those failure surfaces independently with model-only and reliability-only configurations.

papers.title: MARS: A Momentum-Aware Adaptive Rating System for Personalized Assessment
papers.authors: Sahu, Vikrant, Naik, Khethavath Sunil, Gupta, Gagan Raj
papers.abstract: Adaptive assessment systems personalize learning by estimating learner proficiency and recommending suitable questions. However, many existing approaches rely on fixed difficulty labels, static rating updates, or black-box prediction models that provide limited control over rating stability, interpretability, and time-constrained routing. This paper proposes MARS, a Momentum-Aware Adaptive Rating System for interpretable adaptive assessment. MARS represents the question bank as a directed weighted knowledge graph and updates learner proficiency using dynamic rating sensitivity, response quality, and momentum-aware learner velocity. We also formulate a time-budgeted mark-maximization objective in which the policy selects questions within a fixed test duration under negative marking. Experiments on ASSISTments 2009 and MARS-SimExam evaluate MARS for prediction, rating stability, and adaptive routing. Results show that MARS provides smoother rating updates than Fixed Elo and achieves the highest score under time-budgeted negative-marking routing, improving the total score by 8.09 over the strongest baseline and reducing overtime violations from 50% to 5.6%. These results suggest that MARS is suitable for real-time, interpretable, and deployment-friendly adaptive assessment.
papers.summary: MARS combines a question knowledge graph with momentum-sensitive proficiency updates and time-budgeted routing. In its negative-marking experiment, overtime violations fell from 50% to 5.6%. The evaluation concerns adaptive assessment rather than media recommendation.
papers.key_insight: The rate at which a user state changes can inform the next decision. MARS links rating stability to reward and remaining time, offering a transferable idea for budget-constrained personalization.
